1Key Definitions

  • Urbanisation: The increasing proportion of a country's population living in towns and cities.
  • Urban Growth: The absolute increase in the physical size and total population of a city.
  • Urban Sprawl: The uncontrolled outward expansion of a city into the surrounding countryside.
  • Rural-Urban Fringe (RUF): The transition zone where the city meets the countryside (mixed land use).

Squatter Settlement (Slum): Unplanned, informal housing built illegally with poor materials and lacking basic services.

2Causes of Urban Growth

  • Rural-Urban Migration: Driven by Push Factors (drought, poverty, lack of services in the countryside) and Pull Factors (jobs, education, healthcare in the city).

Natural Increase: Birth rates are higher than death rates because cities often have a youthful, reproductive-age population.

Case Study – Nairobi, Kenya (Causes of Growth)

  • Population: 5.5 million (2024), growing at 4–5% annually.
  • Push Factors: Rural poverty, agricultural droughts, and limited access to healthcare (only 30% of rural residents have a health facility within 5km).

Pull Factors: Jobs (Nairobi contributes over 50% of Kenya's GDP), education (home to top universities), and healthcare (doctor-to-patient ratio of 1:1,000 vs. 1:5,000 in rural areas).

3Urban Opportunities vs. Challenges

Opportunities (Positives)Challenges (Negatives)
Economic: Better jobs, higher wages, informal sector opportunities.Housing: Severe shortages lead to slums/squatter settlements.
Social: Better access to education, healthcare, and entertainment.Services: Infrastructure (water, sewage, electricity) cannot keep up.
Growth: Cities drive national economic growth.Inequality: Massive wealth gap between rich and poor neighborhoods.


  • Transport: Severe traffic congestion.

Environment: Pollution and poor waste management.

Case Study – Nairobi, Kenya (Challenges)

  • Slums: About 40% of Nairobi's population (2 million people) live in informal settlements, occupying just 1% of residential land.
  • Kibera: One of Africa's largest slums (estimates range from 170,000 to nearly 1 million residents).
  • Inequality: Nairobi has two billionaires and 5,000 millionaires, yet two-thirds of residents live below $1 a day.

Transport: Severe congestion due to a lack of formal public transport (dominated by unregulated Matatu minibuses).

4Impact on the Rural-Urban Fringe RUF

  • Loss of Agricultural Land: Cities expand into valuable farmland.
  • Environmental Damage: Natural habitats are destroyed; impermeable concrete surfaces increase flood risk.

Social Segregation: Poor slums are pushed to the edges, cut off from city services and jobs.

5Managing Urban Growth (Strategies)

Case Study – Nairobi, Kenya (Management Strategies)

  • Land Tenure (KISIP): The Kenya Informal Settlements Improvement Project maps slums and issues certificates of occupancy. This gives residents legal rights and encourages them to invest in their homes.
  • Affordable Housing Programme: A scheme to build 500,000 affordable homes across Kenya (10,000 built in Nairobi by 2024).
  • Transport Upgrades: Building a BRT (Bus Rapid Transit) system to replace the aggressive, unregulated Matatu minibuses.

Community-Led Projects: Over 10,000 latrine toilets built through output-based subsidies; community water and sanitation projects benefiting thousands of residents.

Alternative Management Strategies (from other cities)

StrategyHow it WorksExample
Self-Help SchemesGovernment provides cheap materials and training; residents build their own homes.Brazil (Vila Verde, Curitiba)
Site & Service SchemesGovernment provides plots with basic services; residents build their own houses.Brazil (Sao Paulo)
Forced EvictionsSlums cleared for development.Lagos, Nigeria (2018 Soweto East eviction displaced 3,000 people)
Public-Private PartnershipsPrivate investors fund redevelopment in exchange for land/profit.Mumbai, India (Dharavi Redevelopment Plan, $2.5 billion)

1Earth's Structure & Plate Tectonics

The Layers (Inside → Out)

  • Inner Core: Solid iron/nickel. Extremely hot.
  • Outer Core: Liquid iron/nickel. Generates magnetic field.
  • Mantle: Semi-molten rock (magma). Contains the Asthenosphere (weak, putty-like layer where convection currents occur).
  • Crust/Lithosphere: Thin, solid rock. Broken into tectonic plates.
  • Oceanic Crust: Thin (~7km), dense (sinks/subducts).
  • Continental Crust: Thick (~35km), less dense (floats).

Why Plates Move

  • Convection Currents: Heat from the core causes magma to rise, cool, and sink, dragging plates.
  • Slab Pull: Dense oceanic plates sink at subduction zones, pulling the rest of the plate down.
  • Ridge Push: New magma at constructive boundaries pushes plates apart.

2The Four Plate Boundaries

Boundary TypeMovementHazardsLandforms
Constructive (Divergent)Plates move apart.Small earthquakes, gentle volcanic eruptions.Mid-ocean ridges, Rift valleys. (e.g., Mid-Atlantic Ridge, Iceland).
Destructive (Convergent)Oceanic plate subducts under continental.Powerful earthquakes, explosive volcanoes, tsunamis.Deep ocean trenches, Composite volcanoes. (e.g., Andes, Ring of Fire).
Collision (Convergent)Two continental plates collide.Powerful earthquakes. No volcanoes (no subduction).Fold mountains. (e.g., Himalayas).
Conservative (Transform)Plates slide past each other.Powerful, frequent earthquakes. No volcanoes.Fault lines. (e.g., San Andreas Fault).


3Earthquakes

Key Terms

  • Focus: The point underground where the earthquake starts.
  • Epicentre: The point directly above the focus on the Earth's surface (where shaking is worst).
  • Seismic Waves: P-waves (fast, arrive first), S-waves (slower, only land), Surface waves (most destructive).

Measurement

  • Richter / Moment Magnitude Scale: Measures magnitude (energy released) on a logarithmic scale (each number is 10x stronger).
  • Mercalli Scale: Measures intensity (observed damage/impact).

Hazards

  • Primary: Ground shaking, surface cracking, building collapse.
  • Secondary: Liquefaction (water-saturated soil turns to liquid), tsunamis, landslides, fires (from broken gas lines).

Case Study – Sulawesi Earthquake 2018 NEE

  • Location: Palu, on the island of Sulawesi, Indonesia.
  • Tectonics: 7.5 magnitude earthquake on the Palu-Koru fault (conservative boundary), at a shallow depth of 10km.
  • Secondary Hazards: A tsunami (5-7m high) and severe liquefaction (which destroyed Petobo village, killing 2,000).
  • Deaths: 4,340 people.
  • Economic Cost: $3 billion.

Management Failure: No tsunami early warning system was operating; no hazard mapping for liquefaction existed.

4Volcanoes

Types of Volcanoes

FeatureShield VolcanoComposite (Strato) Volcano
ShapeBroad, flatSteep, conical
LavaRunny, low viscosityThick, high viscosity
EruptionGentle (effusive)Explosive
BoundaryConstructiveDestructive
ExampleIceland, HawaiiMount St. Helens, Fuji


Volcanic Hazards

  • Pyroclastic Flow: Fast-moving, superheated gas and ash (up to 700°C, 700km/h). Most deadly.
  • Lahar: Volcanic mudflow (ash + water). Buries towns.
  • Ash Fall: Collapses roofs, kills crops, disrupts aviation.
  • Lava Flow: Destroys property but is slow enough to outrun.
  • Toxic Gases: CO2 and SO2 suffocate people.

Case Study – Grindavík / Reykjanes Eruption 2023–25 HIC

  • Location: Reykjanes Peninsula, southwest Iceland (Mid-Atlantic Ridge, constructive boundary).
  • Warning Signs: Over 20,000 earthquakes caused by rising magma before the eruption.
  • Evacuation: 3,790 residents evacuated from Grindavík on 10 November 2023.
  • Deaths/Damage: Only 1 death (ground collapse, not lava). 3 houses destroyed by lava; 50 damaged by earthquakes.
  • Infrastructure: Lava destroyed water pipes supplying 28,000 people.
  • Management (Technique): 14km of earth and rock barriers (up to 8m high) to divert lava from the Svartsengi power station.

Management (Prediction): Extensive monitoring (GPS, tiltmeters, drones) to map ground deformation.

5Why People Live in Hazardous Areas

BenefitExplanation
Fertile SoilVolcanic ash is rich in nutrients, perfect for farming (e.g., Indonesia).
Geothermal EnergyHeat from magma provides cheap, renewable energy (e.g., Iceland).
TourismVolcanoes attract millions of visitors, creating jobs (e.g., Blue Lagoon).
MineralsVolcanic areas are rich in gold, silver, and copper.
Geographical InertiaPeople are tied to their homes, family, and culture.


6Managing Tectonic Hazards

Strategies and Techniques

StrategyTechniqueExample
MonitoringSeismometers (vibrations), Tiltmeters/GPS (ground swelling), Gas sensors (SO2 increase).Iceland's monitoring of Grindavík before the eruption.
PredictionForecasting eruptions (weeks/months in advance). Earthquakes cannot be predicted.Icelandic Meteorological Office issuing warnings.
Protection (Seismic Design)Base isolators (rubber bearings), cross-bracing, reinforced concrete, tsunami walls, lava barriers.14km of lava barriers in Grindavík.
PlanningLand-use zoning (don't build on fault lines), evacuation drills, emergency shelters.Evacuation of 3,790 residents in Grindavík.


Why LICs Suffer More

  • Poor building quality (collapses easily).
  • Lack of money for monitoring, warnings, and emergency response.
  • Slow response due to damaged infrastructure.

1Measuring Development

Development is the political, social, economic, and environmental conditions that influence the quality of life.

Key Indicators

TypeIndicatorWhat It Measures
EconomicGDP, GNIWealth (value of goods/services produced).
SocialLife ExpectancyAverage age people are expected to live.


Literacy Rate Percentage of adults who can read/write.

Infant Mortality Deaths of babies under 1 per 1,000 births.

Doctors per 1,000 Access to healthcare.

CompositeHDI (Human Development Index)Combines life expectancy, education (years of schooling), and GNI per capita. Scored 0 to 1.


Limitations of Indicators

  • Economic indicators are averages and hide inequality within a country.
  • Single indicators (e.g., literacy) only measure one aspect of development.
  • HDI is the best overall measure, but it still lacks a measure of environmental sustainability.

2The Development Gap (Why countries are uneven)

The gap between HICs (High-Income Countries) and LICs (Low-Income Countries) is caused by several interconnected factors:

CategoryCauses of the Development Gap
HistoricalColonialism (wealth stripped), the slave trade, and lasting political instability.
EnvironmentalLandlocked countries (no sea trade), extreme climates (droughts/floods), vulnerability to natural disasters.
EconomicOver-reliance on exporting low-value raw materials (e.g., coffee/cocoa); unfair trade rules; heavy debt burdens.
SocialPoor education/healthcare leads to a low-skilled workforce; high birth rates (poverty trap).
PoliticalCorruption, weak government institutions, and civil conflict/war.


Case Study – Honduras (Reasons for Underdevelopment)

  • Location: Central America (bordered by Guatemala, El Salvador, Nicaragua).
  • Classification: Lower-Middle Income Country (GNI per capita of $3,400 in 2024).
  • Historical: Spanish colonialism stripped wealth and created unequal land ownership.
  • Environmental: Hurricane Mitch (1998) destroyed infrastructure and set the economy back years.
  • Political: Corruption and weak institutions; high crime rates (gangs like MS-13).
  • Economic: Over-reliance on agriculture (coffee, bananas), which is vulnerable to climate change and market fluctuations.

Social: Low levels of education (especially in rural areas) and high inequality (Gini coefficient 50-55).

3Sustainable Development

  • Definition (Brundtland Report): "Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs."
  • The SDGs (Sustainable Development Goals): 17 UN goals (e.g., No Poverty, Zero Hunger, Climate Action) that act as a blueprint for global sustainability.

Circular Economy: Moving away from the linear "Take, Make, Waste" model to a system where resources are reused, recycled, and kept in use for as long as possible.

4Strategies to Reduce the Gap

A. Types of Aid

TypeDescriptionExample
Short-term (Crisis) AidImmediate help after a disaster (food, shelter).Hurricane Mitch relief in Honduras.
Long-term (Development) AidProjects to build infrastructure, schools, or hospitals.Maternal mortality clinics in Honduras.
Top-Down AidLarge-scale government projects (e.g., big dams). Often expensive and can be corrupt.Large infrastructure projects.
Bottom-Up AidSmall-scale, community-led projects (e.g., building wells). More sustainable and targeted.Fair Trade Premium investments (Capucas, Honduras).


B. Debt Relief

Organizations like the World Bank and IMF cancel or reduce a country's debt (e.g., the HIPC Initiative).

Impact: Frees up government money to spend on healthcare and education instead of paying interest.

Case Study – Honduras (Debt Relief)

  • Amount: $1.5 billion in 2005 (HIPC initiative), roughly 50% of its external debt.

Impact: Freed up money to increase the education budget from 7.5% (2005) to 16.4% (2024).

C. Trade & Intermediate Technology

  • Fair Trade: Guarantees farmers in LICs a fair minimum price for their goods (e.g., coffee, cocoa), preventing them from being exploited by global market price drops.
  • Micro-finance: Small loans given to individuals (often women) to start their own businesses.

Intermediate Technology: Simple, affordable, and locally repairable technology (e.g., solar panels, fuel-efficient stoves).

Case Study – Honduras (Fair Trade)

  • Location: Capucas village, Honduras.
  • Scale: Approximately 100,000 Fair Trade coffee farmers in Honduras.
  • Key Mechanism: The Fair Trade Premium (an additional payment to a community fund) provides $3–5 million a year to communities.

Impact: The Capucas community used the premium to build a health center, computer lab, and soccer field. This supports long-term development and improves quality of life.

1Coastal Processes & Waves

Erosion (4 types)

  • Hydraulic Action: Force of water traps air in cracks, breaking rock.
  • Abrasion: Rocks scrape the cliff face (sandpaper effect).
  • Attrition: Rocks smash into each other, becoming smaller and rounder.
  • Solution: Seawater dissolves certain rocks (limestone/chalk).

Transportation

  • Longshore Drift (LSD): The zig-zag movement of sediment along the coast (swash at an angle, backwash straight down).
  • Wave Refraction: Waves bend as they approach a headland, concentrating energy on the headland sides and spreading it out in the bays.
FeatureConstructive WavesDestructive Waves
EnergyLow energyHigh energy
Swash vs. BackwashStrong swash, weak backwashWeak swash, strong backwash
Effect on BeachBuilds up beaches (gently sloping)Erodes beaches (steep profile)


2Coastal Landforms

A. Erosional Landforms (Caused by Destructive Waves)

  • Headlands & Bays: Caused by differential erosion (alternating bands of hard and soft rock). Soft rock erodes fast (bays); hard rock remains (headlands).

Cliffs & Wave-cut Platforms: 1Waves erode the cliff base, creating a wave-cut notch→2The unsupported cliff collapses and retreats→3The flat bedrock left behind is the platform

Cave → Arch → Stack → Stump: Waves attack a weakness (crack) in a headland to form a cave. Erosion goes through to form an arch. The roof collapses to leave an isolated stack. The stack erodes at the base and collapses to leave a stump.

B. Depositional Landforms (Caused by Constructive Waves & LSD)

  • Beaches: Formed by constructive waves. Can be sandy (gentle slope) or shingle (steeper slope).
  • Spits: 1LSD transports sediment along the coast→2When the coastline changes direction (e.g., at a river mouth), LSD continues out to sea, depositing a ridge of sand→3It often ends in a recurve (hook)→4A salt marsh forms in the sheltered water behind it

Sand Dunes (Succession): Form behind the beach. Sequence: Embryo (pioneer plants trap sand)→Yellow (marram grass dominates)→Grey (soil forms, more plant variety)→Mature (trees/shrubs)

3Coastal Management & Case Study

TypeTechniqueProsCons
HardSea WallsStrong protectionExpensive; reflects wave energy (erodes beach).
HardGroynesTraps LSD sediment (builds beach)Causes downdrift erosion further down the coast.
HardRiprap (Rock Armour)Absorbs wave energyExpensive; ugly; rocks can be moved by storms.
SoftBeach NourishmentNatural look; builds a bufferNeeds repeating; expensive.
SoftDune RegenerationNatural; creates habitatsTakes time; easily damaged.
SoftManaged RetreatCheapest; creates salt marsh habitatLand is lost; compensation for landowners.


CASE STUDY: Mappleton (Coastal Erosion Management – HIC)

  • Location: Holderness Coast, East England (population 419).
  • The Problem: Soft boulder clay cliffs retreating at 2m/year (fastest in Europe).
  • The Strategy: "Hold the Line" to protect the town and the vital A-road.
  • The Techniques: Riprap (rock armour) at the cliff base and two riprap groynes.
  • Cost: £2 million.
  • Evaluation (Positive): Successfully built up the beach and protected the town.

Evaluation (Negative): Caused severe downdrift erosion at Great Cowden (starving beaches further south of sediment), increasing erosion rates there.

4Marine Ecosystems & Case Study

FeatureMangroves (Tropical coasts)Coral Reefs (Tropical oceans)
ConditionsSaline, muddy, intertidal zones.Warm (>18°C), shallow, clear, saline water.
ImportanceCoastal protection, biodiversity nursery, carbon sink.Biodiversity hotspot, coastal protection, tourism.
ThreatsCleared for shrimp farms, urban development.Coral Bleaching (warming water), pollution, destructive fishing.
ManagementReplanting, protected areas.Marine Protected Areas (MPAs), strict tourism caps.


CASE STUDY: Gardens of the Queen (Coral Reef Management – HIC)

  • Location: Off the southern coast of Cuba, Caribbean Sea.
  • Status: Largest marine protected area in the Caribbean (2,170 km²), established in 1996.
  • Protection: Commercial fishing is banned; catch-and-release sport fishing is allowed.
  • Tourism Management: Scuba diving is heavily capped at <3,000 divers per year, with sub-surface moorings to avoid anchor damage.
  • Threats: Warming sea temperatures (increased by >0.6°C), causing coral bleaching.

Evaluation: Highly successful due to strict enforcement and science-based management, but still threatened by global climate change.

5Tropical Storms (Hazards)

  • Formation Conditions: Warm ocean (>27°C), between 5° and 30° latitude (Coriolis effect creates spin), deep water.

Main Hazards: High winds, heavy rain, and Storm Surges (unusual rise in sea level pushed ashore by wind, causing severe flooding).

Management

  • Prediction: Satellites, track paths.
  • Preparation: Evacuation drills, early warning systems.
  • Protection: Storm shelters, cyclone-proof buildings.

1Drainage Basin & The Water Cycle

Key Features

  • Source: Where the river begins.
  • Mouth: Where the river meets the sea or a lake.
  • Tributary: A smaller river joining the main channel.
  • Confluence: The point where two rivers meet.
  • Watershed: The boundary of the drainage basin (usually high land).

The System

  • Inputs: Precipitation (rain, snow).
  • Stores: Interception (leaves), Soil moisture, Groundwater.
  • Transfers (Flows): Infiltration (into soil), Percolation (into rock), Throughflow (through soil), Groundwater flow (through rock), Surface runoff (over ground), Channel flow (in river).
  • Outputs: Evaporation, Transpiration (from plants), Evapotranspiration (combined).

2River Processes

Erosion HAAS

  • Hydraulic Action: Force of water traps air in cracks, breaking rock.
  • Abrasion: Rocks scrape the bed/banks (sandpaper effect).
  • Attrition: Rocks smash into each other, becoming smaller and rounder.
  • Solution: Acidic water dissolves rock (limestone/chalk).

Transportation TSSS

  • Traction: Large rocks rolled along the bed.
  • Saltation: Small pebbles bounce along the bed.
  • Suspension: Fine particles carried within the water.
  • Solution: Dissolved material carried invisibly.

Deposition

  • Occurs when the river loses energy (slower flow, shallow water, meeting the sea).
  • Heaviest material is deposited first.

3Changes Downstream (Bradshaw Model)

CharacteristicUpstream (Upper)Downstream (Lower)
Discharge (volume of water)LowHigh
Channel Width & DepthNarrow & ShallowWide & Deep
Velocity (speed)Slow (high friction)Fast (smooth bed)
Load QuantityLowHigh
Load Particle SizeLarge, angularSmall, round
Gradient (slope)SteepGentle
Bed RoughnessRoughSmooth


4Landforms

Upper Course (Vertical Erosion)

  • V-shaped Valleys: River cuts down vertically. Weathering and mass movement widen the top.
  • Interlocking Spurs: River winds around hard rock.
  • Waterfalls & Gorges: 1Hard rock over soft rock→2Soft rock erodes (hydraulic action/abrasion), creating an overhang→3Plunge pool forms→4Overhang collapses→5Waterfall retreats upstream, leaving a steep-sided gorge
  • Potholes: Pebbles swirl in eddies on the riverbed, eroding hollows.

Middle Course (Lateral Erosion)

  • Meanders: 1Helicoidal flow→2Faster water on the outside bend causes erosion (river cliff)→3Slower water on the inside bend causes deposition (slip-off slope)
  • Oxbow Lakes: 1Erosion narrows the meander neck→2A flood breaches the neck→3Deposition seals off the old meander

Lower Course (Deposition)

  • Floodplains: Flat land either side of the river formed by repeated flooding and deposition of alluvium.
  • Levees: Natural raised banks formed by coarse sediment dropped during floods.
  • Deltas: Form at the mouth when the river meets still water (sea/lake) and deposits sediment faster than it can be removed.
  • Arcuate: Fan-shaped, many distributaries (e.g., Nile). Tide-dominated.
  • Cuspate: Tooth-shaped, few distributaries (e.g., Ebro). Wave-dominated.
  • Bird's Foot: Long, finger-like distributaries (e.g., Mississippi). River-dominated.

5Flooding & Management

Causes of Flooding

  • Physical: Prolonged/heavy rain, snowmelt, steep slopes, impermeable rock, saturated ground.
  • Human: Urbanisation (impermeable concrete), deforestation (less interception), agriculture (compacted soil).
  • Flood Hydrograph: Shows Lag Time (delay between peak rainfall and peak discharge) and Peak Discharge (max volume of water).

Management Strategies

Hard Engineering (Man-made)Soft Engineering (Natural)Adaptive (Living with floods)
Dams: Store water, HEP (Expensive, displaces people).Afforestation: Planting trees increases interception.Early Warning: Alerts to evacuate.
Channelisation: Straightening (Faster flow, floods downstream).Floodplain Zoning: Banning building in high-risk areas.Floodplain Zoning: Similar to soft.
Levees/Embankments: Raised walls (Can breach catastrophically).River Restoration: Re-meandering, reconnecting floodplains.Sandbags: Temporary barriers.


Case Study – Three Gorges Dam (River Management – NEE)

  • Location: Yangtze River, Hubei province, central China.
  • Scale: 181m high, 600km reservoir, cost $31 billion (opened 2012).
  • Flood Protection: Reduces major downstream flooding from 1-in-10 years to 1-in-100 years.
  • Cities Protected: Wuhan, Nanjing, and Shanghai.
  • Historical Context: Designed to prevent disasters like the 1954 flood (killed 33,169 people).

Negative Impact: Displaced 1.3 million people; altered sediment flow causing downstream erosion.

Case Study – Belgian Floods 2021 (River Flood – HIC)

  • Location: River Vesdre (Meuse tributary), Ardennes, southeast Belgium.
  • Cause: A "water bomb" dropped 93mm of rain in 24 hours onto already saturated soils (15 July 2021).
  • Deaths: 41 people died (21 in the Vesdre catchment).
  • Economic Cost: $2.8 billion.
  • Damage: Over 200 bridges damaged/destroyed; water/gas/electricity supplies cut.
  • Strategy (Macro): BE-Alert early warning system (but failed for those asleep/no phone).
  • Technique (Physical): Adaptive urban design (widening floodplains, converting ground floors to parking).

Sustainable Technique: River restoration (reconnecting the river to its floodplain at 10 sites).

1Key Definitions

TermDefinition
Birth RateLive births per 1,000 people per year.
Death RateDeaths per 1,000 people per year.
Natural IncreaseBirth rate is higher than death rate (population grows).
Fertility RateAverage number of children per woman.
Replacement Level2.1 (The rate needed to maintain population size).
Dependency RatioRatio of dependents (under 15 + over 65) to the working-age population (15–64).


2The Demographic Transition Model DTM

Shows how population changes over time as a country develops.

StageBirth RateDeath RatePopulationExample
1. High FluctuatingHighHighStableRemote tribes
2. Early ExpandingHighFalling fastRapid growthNigeria
3. Late ExpandingFallingLowSlowing growthBrazil
4. Low FluctuatingLowLowStableUSA
5. DecliningVery LowLowShrinkingJapan, Germany


Limitations of DTM: Assumes all countries follow the same path; doesn't account for migration or sudden events (wars/pandemics).

3Population Structure (Pyramids)

FeatureYouthful Population (LICs)Ageing Population (HICs)
Pyramid ShapeWide base, narrow topNarrow base, wide top
CausesHigh birth rates, falling death ratesLow birth rates, long life expectancy
ExampleNigeriaJapan
ImpactsPositives: Future workforce.
Negatives: High dependency ratio, pressure on schools/hospitals.Positives: Experienced workforce.


Negatives: Labour shortages, high pension/healthcare costs.

4Population Policies

FeaturePro-natalist (Encourage Births)Anti-natalist (Reduce Births)
Why use it?Ageing population, labour shortagesOverpopulation, resource strain
StrategiesBaby bonuses, generous parental leave, free childcareLegal restrictions (fines), contraception access, girls' education
Example 1Japan: New Angel Plan (1999), Four-day workweek (2025). Evaluation: Modest success.China: One-Child Policy (1979–2016). Evaluation: Reduced births, but caused gender imbalance & ageing crisis.
Example 2Czech Republic: 3-year parental leave, tax incentives. Evaluation: Most successful in Europe.Nigeria: Tries to reduce fertility but fails (Demographic Trap). Evaluation: Poverty and cultural preferences maintain high birth rates.


5International Migration

Types of Migrants

  • Economic Migrant: Moves voluntarily for work/better pay.
  • Refugee: Forced to flee (war/persecution); has legal status.
  • Asylum Seeker: Has fled, but waiting for legal refugee status.

Push & Pull Factors

Push Factors (Leave)Pull Factors (Attract)
Poverty, unemployment, war, natural disastersJobs, higher wages, better healthcare, family connections


Impacts of Migration

On Origin (Country of Origin)On Destination (Host Country)
➕ Remittances (money sent home) boosts the economy.➕ Fills labour shortages (especially low-skilled jobs).
➕ Reduced pressure on local jobs.➕ Cultural diversity.
➖ Brain Drain (loss of skilled workers).➖ Pressure on housing, schools, and hospitals.
➖ Family separation.➖ Social tension / perceived job competition.


Managing Migration

  • Border Controls: Fences, patrols (e.g., Ceuta and Melilla).
  • Reception Centres: Processing asylum seekers.
  • Seasonal Work Visas: Legal migration for agriculture.
  • Development Aid: Improving origin countries to reduce the need to leave.
